title: Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
content:
Meta says it’s issuing a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives. As part of its third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, the company says the non-voting stock will also go toward potential acquisitions and employee compensation, with trading beginning in 2027.
Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
Meta says the new class of shares will also fund acquisitions and employee compensation.
“The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant,” Meta says in the press release. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, added during an earnings call that the new class of shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.”
Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion and $145 billion estimate.
It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September. Like other AI agents, Muse can do things like clean out your email inbox, book restaurant reservations, and plan trips. The Muse app shot to the top of app stores shortly after its rollout, and hit 10 million downloads in the US this week. Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week.
Muse’s launch hasn’t come without some snags. Amid concerns about user privacy, a tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The company has also had to pause Muse’s conversation-sharing feature after researchers discovered chats publicly available on the web.

report.summary: Meta will issue a new non-voting share class, trading in 2027, to fund AI investments, acquisitions, and employee compensation as capex rises to $135–$145 billion.
report.background: Meta’s move comes amid an industry-wide race to build AI infrastructure, hire scarce talent, and launch consumer AI products. The company has been spending heavily on data centers, AI models, and talent poaching, and its third-quarter earnings report shows those costs continuing to climb. By creating a new non-voting share class, Meta is trying to broaden its financing options without relying solely on cash flow or debt as AI competition intensifies. The timing reflects both the capital intensity of frontier AI and Meta’s need to keep funding acquisitions and employee compensation. The shares will not trade until 2027, so the announcement is more about future financial flexibility than immediate cash. It also signals that AI spending is becoming a structural part of Meta’s capital strategy, not a one-off budget item.
key_points: Meta announced the new non-voting share class in its third-quarter earnings report. The stock is intended to fund AI initiatives, potential acquisitions, and employee compensation, with trading expected to begin in 2027.

Meta says the investment scale needed to compete, grow, expand infrastructure, and pursue AI initiatives is significant. CFO Susan Li said the shares expand funding tools and provide flexibility behind AI-driven momentum across the business.

Meta raised its 2026 capital expenditure outlook to $135 billion–$145 billion, up from a prior $130 billion–$145 billion range. The increase underscores how expensive data centers, compute, and AI talent have become.

Meta launched its Muse AI agent in September. It can clean email inboxes, book reservations, and plan trips, and Meta says the app hit 10 million US downloads this week. Meta also rolled out the Muse Wonder model.

Muse’s rollout has run into privacy and security problems. A YouTuber reported the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace, and Meta paused a conversation-sharing feature after researchers found chats publicly available on the web.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta’s new share class could normalize creative equity financing for massive AI capex, reinforcing that frontier AI is a capital-markets game as much as a research race. For developers, Meta’s continued spending may mean more compute, models, and agent platforms to build on, but also more scrutiny of agent permissions and data handling. For regular users, expect more capable AI agents like Muse, but also more visible privacy and safety failures as these products scale quickly. The key test is whether Meta can convert huge spending and flexible financing into reliable products without repeating Muse’s early privacy missteps.
report.tools: To follow the agent trend, watch Meta AI and the Muse app, plus the Muse Wonder model. For hands-on experimentation, try open-source agent frameworks such as LangChain, AutoGen, and OpenHands, and use browser or privacy sandboxes to test agent permissions and data access before trusting them with personal accounts.
